source.title: Anchoring Refusal Direction: Mitigating Safety Risks in Tuning via Projection Constraint
source.authors: Yan-Rui Du; Feng-Lei Fan; Sen-Dong Zhao; Jia-Wei Cao; Qi-Ka Lin; Kai He; Ting Liu; Bing Qin; Meng-Ling Feng

record.tranche_reason: The study uses the difference-in-means refusal direction and intervenes on its projections during fine-tuning, then measures safety outcomes. This conceptually tests whether maintaining the direction affects safety, but it does not perform the original direct ablation or addition intervention.
record.gate_note: The paper reports its own projection-constraint training results, safety evaluations, task accuracy, and refusal-direction drift. Results cited from other studies about directly amplifying or ablating the direction are not recorded as this paper's findings. The main tables report aggregate safety rates; detailed individual attack-type ASRs and comparisons of unrelated defense methods are left out.
record.test_reason: The study takes the Arditi et al. difference-in-means direction as given and uses it as an anchor for a fine-tuning regularizer (ProCon). Its results compare its own method against plain IFT and other defenses: aggregate ASR, HS and task accuracy. It never ablates the direction or adds it to activations to test whether it mediates refusal. It also never checks whether capabilities survive such an intervention. Lower ASR under the projection constraint is weak, indirect evidence at best. It is confounded by the extra 1k safety samples in the _safe variants and by warm-up schedules. It is a method-performance result, not a test of V1–V8. The one direction-level finding (drift of the direction during IFT, Fig. 2, Fig. 3) is a related construct and is recorded under fits_no_version.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors hypothesize ('guess') that refusal-direction drift during IFT is one of the main causes of safety loss. They take the safety gains of their projection-constraint method as support for that hypothesis. They present ProConwu_safe (strong early constraint plus 1k safety samples) as reducing drift and ASR while keeping task accuracy. They do not test the refusal direction's causal role itself; they cite Arditi et al. for it.
record.recipe_differences: The study identifies the direction using the difference-in-means approach, but its intervention regularizes training-sample projections during IFT rather than directly ablating or adding the direction.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper reports that constraint strength trades off safety and task performance; the strongest drift occurs early in training; the number of warm-up epochs differs across models (approximately four for LLaMA2 and LLaMA3 and around sixteen for Qwen2); adding safety-oriented data can reduce the required warm-up duration by about half.

fits_no_version.finding: The difference-in-means refusal direction drifts during benign instruction fine-tuning in LLaMA2-7B, LLaMA3-8B and Qwen2-7B. Cosine to the initial direction falls with training, most sharply after the first epoch and most in deeper layers (middle layers for Qwen2). This coincides with rising ASR. Constraining projections onto the initial direction reduces drift and ASR.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Instruction fine-tuning rotates the refusal direction (drift), and this drift contributes to fine-tuning-induced loss of refusal.

record.problems: The study does not directly ablate or add the refusal direction to test refusal behavior. It reports no uncertainty estimates or significance tests. Several direction-drift and constraint-level results are presented only in figures without exact values in the text.
record.rows_left_out: Detailed per-attack ASR results in Tables VIII-XI and HS scores in Tables I-IV are not separately included because aggregate ASR rows are recorded for the main safety outcome. Results for comparison methods that do not intervene on or measure the refusal direction are omitted.

untested.parts: No ablation of the direction, no addition of it to induce refusal on harmless prompts, and no capability check under such interventions. The direction is only used as a training regularizer target.

missing.what: Drift of the refusal direction across 10 epochs of plain IFT, per layer, for all three models: the core observational result. No row records it, though it underlies the fits_no_version finding. Values are figure-only.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's 'tests/T2' and V1 'supports' labels are not justified. The paper never performs the ablation or addition interventions V1 names, and all ASR rows are own-method-vs-baseline comparisons. The reader's label reason also contained a typo ('r24-r20'). ASR is a rule-based refusal-phrase metric; HS is judged by GPT-4o. No uncertainty is reported. Results cited in the paper about amplifying or ablating the direction come from Arditi et al. [16], not from this study.

versions.untested_parts: Does not directly ablate the direction at every layer and position or add it to induce refusals to harmless requests. Safety tests use harmfulness scores and attack success rates, not a separate harmless-request refusal rate. Task accuracy is the reported capability measure.
No weight edit or released-model abliteration experiment.
The attack-IFT condition injects affirmative responses to malicious instructions; it does not test attacks that suppress the refusal direction or training against that ablation.
Does not test whether refusal is represented by multiple directions, an affine structure, or a cone.
Does not separate harmfulness judgment from refusal decision.
No cross-language, base-to-instruct, or model-variant transfer test of the direction.
The study examines direction drift during IFT and varies warm-up schedules, but does not test whether training determines the existence of a single removable direction.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Projection-constrained IFT across the tested chat models and IFT settings
reader_labels.reason: Projection-constrained training reduces aggregate ASR relative to IFT and the reported UltraInteract accuracy remains close to the IFT reference (r1-r17, r24-r20, r24-r36).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Strong projection constraints applied throughout training
reader_labels.reason: The paper states that stronger constraints can reduce safety risks further while diminishing task-performance gains; the plotted task results are not numerically stated (r21-r23).
